toc.title: Do you have safe others in your life?
If you don't have anyone yet
Emotional isolation, from others and from yourself

blocks.p: This continues what keeps you stuck. Last time it was your stories. This time it's isolation, and your support system.
We're not going to go over the whole Polyvagal Theory here, but one piece of it is important to understand accurately: co-regulation.

Co-regulation is not just supporting each other. It's not just one person listening to another and offering advice or encouragement. When I say co-regulation, I'm talking about a biological process that happens between two nervous systems. We'll talk about two human beings here, although it happens between you and your pets as well.

Co-regulation is an unconscious, autonomic process. Say we have two people. One is dysregulated, maybe in a very anxious state. They feel anxiety, more of a flight state in their nervous system. The other person is more in a safety state. That means they're able to smile and use eye crinkles. They can listen accurately. They have vocal prosody, a greater range of voice.

The person in their safety state sends cues of safety through all of those little unconscious social signals to the other person, who's in more of a defensive, anxious flight state. That person picks up on it, and it helps them feel safer. That's the basic idea of co-regulation.

We need each other. We are individuals, yes. We have personal responsibility, absolutely. But we're also social creatures. Human beings are mammals, and mammals are social creatures. We can't ignore that aspect of ourselves and live a happy, healthy, full life. Co-regulation and our connection to each other go hand in hand.

blocks.h: Do you have safe others in your life?

blocks.p: Something to reflect on: do you have safe people in your life? Every single one of us needs safe others.
If you exist more in a fight state, an aggressive state, you might think you're fine on your own. "F everybody else. I got this. I don't need anybody."

If you're in more of a shutdown, depressed, numb, isolated state, you might think you'll never find other people. Maybe you've given up on that, whether it's relationships, friendships, or reconnecting with your family if you need to. Or maybe you have safe people in your life, and you think they'll give up on you. Those are the kinds of beliefs we have from a shutdown state.

But you might also have safe people in your life and just be missing it. At the time, I was a therapist in a school district, and I worked with a lot of students who came from homes with little or no co-regulation. They'd come to school, and they didn't like school, but they didn't realize that school gave them opportunities for co-regulation. Sometimes with friends, but a lot of times with staff. There was a teacher, or someone, they could really connect with. When they stopped and thought about it, they realized, "Oh, there is that one person."

So maybe they're there in your life too, and you're missing it. Stop and ask yourself: who do I feel safe around? Who do I feel some trust with, maybe some vulnerability, some calm, some happiness? Who do I smile with, genuine smiles?

That's an opportunity for co-regulation. Maybe it's not somebody in your home. But there might be somebody in your life, even just in little moments. Even in a store, you see somebody and you give each other a smile, and that can help you feel tiny bits of safety. It's not ideal, but it's better than nothing.
Another question, just for your own self-reflection, maybe even for journaling: are you able to identify safety? If you have safe people in your life, can you feel it?

This can be really hard to recognize in others, especially if you don't have a history of co-regulation, of healthy attachment. You might not be able to feel it when it is there. If that's the case, the priority might be to learn how to identify safety, and then build on that.

To identify safety, I think you first have to find it within yourself, especially as you get older. Find it within yourself, then branch out from there and look for friendships and relationships. Identify safety first, and then recognize it in other people.

If you don't do that, and you're mindlessly looking for connection without really feeling the connection, you may be setting yourself up for "friendships" or "relationships" that are not healthy, where you may be taken advantage of, or worse. You may not be finding safety. You may be finding protection instead, or something that feels like protection.

Here's how you tell the difference. When you actually have safety with somebody, you'll be able to smile together and make gentle eye contact. You'll be able to feel vulnerable. That doesn't mean telling them all your stuff. It means that inside, you feel calm. Breathing might be easier.

That's different from just feeling less defensive. If you're around someone and your anxiety is reduced, or your aggression is reduced, or you have more life in you, less numbness, that's something. But it might just be relief from whatever defensive state you're stuck in. It doesn't necessarily mean you're accessing your own safe and social state and connecting with somebody else who's also accessing theirs.

You might feel less defensive with someone who is able to manipulate you into feeling less defensive, without building a solid co-regulating relationship. There's a difference there: safety versus protection.

blocks.h: If you don't have anyone yet

blocks.p: If you don't have anybody in your life, you can find some co-regulation through other means, or professionally. There's lots of co-regulation happening in therapy. Hiring a therapist can be a great way, maybe the first way, to feel safety, vulnerability, and connection, and then build from there. You'll get safe voices and safe faces. Hopefully you get a competent therapist who's able to do that for you.

You can also discover safety through your senses, on your own, if you don't know what safety feels like. What do you see, or smell, or touch? There might be a certain texture that speaks to your system and helps you feel safer, calmer, happier, and breathe easier. There might be a smell, a sight, some piece of your environment or nature, where you feel more safety, more calm, more connectedness, more wholeness. That's a really good way to feel safety within yourself, build from there, and then identify it in other people.

Movement can be a really good way to feel safety. Music is such a good way too. It can help you feel your feelings and eventually climb your [polyvagal ladder](piece:autonomic-nervous-system) into more of a safe and social state.

What absolutely does not help is isolating. I mean physically isolating. A lot of teens go to their room and isolate. That might not be you. But you might isolate in your home, or on your phone. Right now, you might be isolating. Maybe I'm part of the problem. You might isolate with a screen in front of your face and cut out the rest of the world.

That doesn't necessarily help, especially if it's done mindlessly. If you can mindfully use your phone, for meditation or for some visual stimuli, maybe that could help. But otherwise, isolation in general doesn't help.

blocks.h: Emotional isolation, from others and from yourself

blocks.p: What I'm most concerned about for you is emotional isolation. I think it's something we all do. We cut ourselves off emotionally from other people. That could be just keeping your emotions to yourself: someone asks how you're doing, and they mean it, and you say, "I'm fine."

But we also isolate emotionally from ourselves, and that doesn't help either. Hiding your emotions, stuffing them down, minimizing them, rationalizing them, or maximizing and catastrophizing: all the things we do to cut ourselves off from our true felt experience, our true emotions.
Sometimes keeping things to yourself is needed. There are plenty of circumstances where someone just isn't ready to talk about it, even in therapy. That might be justified.

But in general, ignoring how you feel just doesn't help. We have to actually feel our feelings, as we're ready to. It's not always easy. Sometimes it's downright uncomfortable. Sometimes it's downright painful. Sometimes we're not ready for it. If our social engagement system, our safety state, isn't built up enough, then tapping into that defensive state is really hard. It might be extremely uncomfortable. If what you're dealing with is stuck defensive state trauma stuff, delving into it before you're ready could absolutely be re-traumatizing.
But eventually, we have to feel our feelings and stop minimizing or excusing or rationalizing. And once you can feel it, don't make it go away. Just let it be there, and notice as it shifts.

If you can do that mindfully, that will stop the emotional isolation, at least from yourself. If you can focus on what's going on within you, you won't be emotionally cutting yourself off from yourself. From there, maybe you can build, and share it with safe others in your life if you have them, or start to identify safe others.

That doesn't mean I want you to share all your stuff with anybody and everybody. That's not what I mean at all. But the more you can feel safe, and then tap into your stuck defensive energy, the better, in general.
